worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy received its registration and began dispensing on a Monday with no controlled substances on the shelves; its first Schedule II and Schedule IV shipments arrived that Friday. The pharmacist in charge signed a record on the Monday stating that no controlled substances were on hand. Twenty-three months later a new pharmacist in charge reviews the files, decides that the Monday record was not really an inventory because nothing was counted, and proposes to take what he calls the pharmacy's first inventory on the second anniversary of the Friday delivery.
steps: Read what 21 CFR 1304.11(b) attaches the initial inventory to. It is the date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances, which here is the Monday the pharmacy began dispensing and not the Friday the stock arrived.

Give the zero-stock sentence its effect. The same paragraph says that a person who commences business with no controlled substances on hand shall record this fact as the initial inventory, so the Monday record is the initial inventory rather than a substitute for one.

Start the recurring cycle where 21 CFR 1304.11(c) starts it. The biennial duty runs after the initial inventory is taken, so the clock began on the Monday and the next inventory may be taken on any date which is within two years of that date.

Convert that into a date on the calendar. Two years from the Monday, not two years from the Friday delivery, and not two years from whatever later date someone now prefers to describe as the first inventory.

Check the Monday record against the general requirements in 21 CFR 1304.11(a) before relying on it. It must be in written, typewritten or printed form, kept at the registered location, and it must indicate whether it was taken as of opening of business or as of the close of business on that date.
worked_examples.resolution: The Monday zero-stock record is the initial inventory and the two-year cycle runs from it, so the proposed date falls outside the window. The error the scenario invites is treating an inventory that records nothing on hand as no inventory at all, which quietly moves the start of the biennial cycle forward to the first delivery; the detail worth checking either way is whether the record carries the opening or close of business notation 21 CFR 1304.11(a) requires.

worked_examples.scenario: It is inventory day at a retail pharmacy. On the counter sit an unopened 500-tablet bottle of a Schedule II product, an opened 500-tablet bottle of that same Schedule II product, an opened 1,200-capsule bottle of a Schedule IV product, and a partly used stock bottle of a Schedule III product set aside as damaged and awaiting disposal. A technician proposes to estimate everything except the Schedule II items, and suggests decanting the 1,200-capsule bottle into two smaller bottles first so that neither one is over the threshold.
steps: Separate the container-level entries from the counting question. 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6) has the dispenser include the information 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) requires, so the unopened bottle is recorded by its finished form, the units it contains and the number of such containers.

Apply the counting rule only where the paragraph applies it. The exact-or-estimate choice is for determining the number of units of each finished form in a commercial container that has been opened, so it reaches the opened Schedule II bottle and the opened Schedule IV bottle and no others here.
Take the opened Schedule II bottle. A substance listed in Schedules I or II gets an exact count or measure of the contents, and the paragraph attaches no size threshold to that requirement.

Take the opened Schedule IV bottle. Schedules III, IV and V may be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, and 1,200 capsules is more than 1,000, so this one is counted exactly.

Do not lose the damaged Schedule III stock. 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iv), incorporated for dispensers by 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6), calls for the name of the substance, the total quantity and the reason it is being maintained, so it belongs on the inventory even though it will never be dispensed.
worked_examples.resolution: Exact counts for both opened bottles, container-level entries for the unopened one, and a separate entry for the damaged stock. The scenario invites two errors: reading the more-than-1,000 threshold as though it also licensed estimating an opened Schedule II container, and hunting for a repackaging step instead of counting the commercial container that was actually opened.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy's last controlled-substance inventory was taken twenty-five months ago. The pharmacist in charge points out that the store's regular general physical inventory falls next month and argues that federal law lets the controlled-substance count ride along with it. In the same conversation she proposes clearing filing space by shredding inventory records older than eighteen months, on the ground that the pharmacy has taken a newer inventory since.
steps: Fix the deadline before weighing the argument. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) requires a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years and permits any date which is within two years of the previous biennial inventory date, so month twenty-five is already outside the limit.

Read the statute the argument leans on. 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) directs that the regulations permit the biennial inventory to be prepared on the registrant's regular general physical inventory date which is nearest to and does not vary by more than six months from the biennial date that would otherwise apply.

Ask what that clause actually does. It tells the rulemaker how to accommodate a business's own stock-taking, and the current regulation implements it by letting the registrant pick any date inside the two-year window. It is not six further months added on top of that window.

Turn to the shredding proposal on its own footing. 21 CFR 1304.04(a) requires every inventory and other record required under part 1304 to be kept and available for inspection and copying for at least 2 years from the date of such inventory or record, so a record eighteen months old is still inside the period.

Notice that a newer inventory does not release an older record. The period in 21 CFR 1304.04(a) runs from each record's own date, so taking a fresh inventory starts a new period without ending the one already running.
worked_examples.resolution: The inventory is overdue now and cannot wait for next month's general stock-take, and the eighteen-month-old records stay. The errors the scenario invites are reading the statutory six-month coordination clause as a grace period added to the regulatory deadline, and treating a newer inventory as something that discharges the retention period still running on an older one.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts owner holds a controlled substance registration for a retail pharmacy and is opening an outsourcing facility in a different city together with a wholesale drug warehouse at a third address. An administrator prepares a single renewal covering all three premises and diaries it against the pharmacy's federal biennial inventory date, reasoning that everything in controlled substances runs on a two-year cycle anchored to the last inventory.
steps: Start with how many registrations are in play. 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances, so three premises means three registrations rather than one renewal.

Take the terms one registrant type at a time under 247 CMR 11.06. The registration issued to a pharmacy is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year, and the registration issued to an outsourcing facility is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year.

Notice where the third registration departs. Under 247 CMR 11.06 the registration issued to a wholesale druggist is valid for one year beginning on December 1st of each year, so it differs from the other two in length and in start date.

Detach the registration term from the inventory clock. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) measures its two years from the registrant's previous biennial inventory date, while 247 CMR 11.06 measures the pharmacy term from January 1st of an even-numbered year, so an inventory date cannot be used to diary a registration.
worked_examples.resolution: Three separate registrations, two of them running two years from January 1st of an even-numbered year and the wholesale one running a single year from December 1st. The errors the scenario invites are folding several principal places of business into one registration, and letting a familiar federal two-year inventory interval stand in for a Massachusetts term that is fixed by the calendar and varies by registrant type.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What event does 21 CFR 1304.11(b) attach the initial inventory to?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy commences business with no controlled substances on hand. What does the initial-inventory paragraph require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That it record this fact as the initial inventory; zero stock produces an inventory rather than excusing one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How often is the biennial inventory required, and which dates are available?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years, on any date which is within two years of the previous biennial inventory date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) say about a registrant's regular general physical inventory date, and what does it not do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It directs that the regulations permit the biennial inventory to be prepared on that date where it is nearest to and does not vary by more than six months from the biennial date that would otherwise apply. It does not add six months to the regulatory limit, which the current regulation states as any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In an opened commercial container, which schedules require an exact count or measure of the contents whatever the container size?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedules I and II.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the threshold that turns an estimate into an exact count for Schedules III, IV and V, in the regulation's own units.
retrieval_prompts.answer: More than 1,000 tablets or capsules in the opened container.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which containers does the exact-or-estimate choice in 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6) apply to?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Only a commercial container that has been opened. An unopened container is captured by the container-level entries 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long must an inventory be kept under 21 CFR 1304.04(a), from when, and in what condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least 2 years from the date of that inventory or record, kept by the registrant and available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does the exception at the front of 21 CFR 1304.04(a) actually change?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Where certain records sit, not how long they are kept. Paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) let financial and shipping records be held centrally, expressly excluding executed order forms, and let a registered retail pharmacy hold the records of its long term care automated dispensing system registrations.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a registrant do before keeping financial and shipping records centrally, and when may it start?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Submit written notification by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, in triplicate, to the Special Agent in Charge in its area; it may maintain central records commencing 14 days after the Special Agent in Charge receives the notification, unless it is informed that permission is denied.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name four things 21 CFR 1304.11(a) requires of every inventory.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any four of: a complete and accurate record of all controlled substances on hand on the date it is taken; maintenance in written, typewritten or printed form; keeping at the registered location; prompt transcription where an oral recording device was used; a separate inventory for each registered location and each independent activity registered; and an indication of whether it was taken as of opening or as of close of business.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is the requirement of a separate registration for each premises a Massachusetts feature?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 21 CFR 1301.12(a) requires a separate DEA registration for each principal place of business, and 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate Board controlled substance registration at each principal place of business.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 do with the federal record and inventory requirements?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It requires registered persons to keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with them, and adds any further rules the Board of Registration in Pharmacy promulgates for a retail drug business or wholesale druggist, or the Commissioner in all other cases.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 11.05, how many controlled substance registrations does one owner need for three principal places of business?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Three. A separate registration is required at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Give the three registration terms set by 247 CMR 11.06.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Pharmacy, two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year; outsourcing facility, two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year; wholesale druggist, one year beginning on December 1st of each year.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two-year period moves with the registrant, and which is fixed by the calendar?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The federal biennial inventory interval moves with the registrant's own previous inventory date; the Massachusetts pharmacy registration term is fixed at January 1st of each even-numbered year.

quick_review.text: Each inventory contains a complete and accurate record of all controlled substances on hand on the date it is taken, and is maintained in written, typewritten or printed form at the registered location.
A separate inventory is made for each registered location and each independent activity registered, except as 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(4) provides.
The inventory may be taken either as of opening of business or as of the close of business on the inventory date, and which one was used shall be indicated on the inventory.

Substances are deemed on hand when they are in the possession of or under the control of the registrant, which reaches substances returned by a customer, ordered but not yet invoiced, stored in a warehouse on the registrant's behalf, or held by employees for distribution as complimentary samples.

A separate DEA registration is required for each principal place of business or professional practice at one general physical location where controlled substances are manufactured, distributed, imported, exported or dispensed.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires registered persons to keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the federal record-keeping and inventory requirements, and with any additional rules the Board promulgates for a retail drug business or wholesale druggist or the Commissioner promulgates in all other cases.
One such Board addition is the Schedule II perpetual inventory in 247 CMR 9.21(8), reconciled at least once every ten days against an accurate physical count, which 21 CFR part 1304 does not require.
The initial inventory is taken on the date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances, and covers all stocks of controlled substances on hand.
A person who commences business with no controlled substances on hand records that fact as the initial inventory, so the duty is discharged by a record rather than skipped.

21 CFR 1304.11(b) takes the initial inventory in accordance with paragraph (e) of the section as applicable, so the content and counting rules that govern a routine inventory govern the first one too.
After the initial inventory is taken, the registrant takes a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years.

The biennial inventory may be taken on any date which is within two years of the previous biennial inventory date, so the outer limit is measured from the last inventory rather than from any anniversary of registration.

21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) coordinates the biennial count with a registrant's regular general physical inventory date within six months of the otherwise applicable biennial date, but it does not authorise delaying the inventory past the regulatory two-year limit.

A dispenser's inventory includes the information required of manufacturers under 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) and (iv), which covers finished-form stock by container as well as damaged, defective or impure substances and stock held for quality control or extemporaneous compounding.
The exact-or-estimate choice applies only in determining the number of units of each finished form in a commercial container that has been opened.
For an opened container, a substance listed in Schedules I or II requires an exact count or measure of the contents, with no size threshold.
For an opened container, a substance listed in Schedule III, IV, or V may be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, in which case an exact count is required.

Every inventory and other record required to be kept under 21 CFR part 1304 must be kept by the registrant and available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration for at least 2 years from the date of that inventory or record.
The two-year period in 21 CFR 1304.04(a) is a floor measured from each record's own date, so a later inventory neither shortens nor absorbs the period still running on an earlier record.
A separate controlled substance registration is required at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances.
A Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a pharmacy or to an outsourcing facility is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year.

A Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a wholesale druggist is valid for one year beginning on December 1st of each year, so it differs from the pharmacy term in both length and start date.

decision_logic.condition: Any controlled-substance inventory is being taken, initial or biennial.
decision_logic.action: Record all substances on hand on that date in written, typewritten or printed form, keep it at the registered location, make it separate for each registered location, and state on its face whether it was taken as of opening or as of close of business.

decision_logic.condition: A registrant is about to begin controlled-substance activity, whether or not stock has arrived.
decision_logic.action: Take the initial inventory on the date activity begins; if no controlled substances are on hand, record that fact as the initial inventory rather than waiting for the first delivery.

decision_logic.condition: The question asks whether a recurring inventory is overdue.
decision_logic.action: Find the previous biennial inventory date and measure two years from it, since 21 CFR 1304.11(c) permits any date within two years of that date and nothing later.

decision_logic.condition: Someone offers a registrant's regular general physical inventory date as a reason to take the controlled-substance count later.
decision_logic.action: Test the proposed date against the regulatory two-year limit first. The statutory coordination in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) does not extend the deadline beyond two years from the previous biennial inventory.

decision_logic.condition: A container is in front of the person taking the inventory.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether the commercial container has been opened. If it has not, record the container-level information; if it has, move to the schedule test in 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6).

decision_logic.condition: The opened container holds a substance listed in Schedules I or II.
decision_logic.action: Make an exact count or measure of the contents, whatever the container size.

decision_logic.condition: The opened container holds a substance listed in Schedule III, IV, or V.
decision_logic.action: Estimate the count or measure, unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, in which case count it exactly.

decision_logic.condition: A controlled-substance record or inventory is being destroyed, archived or migrated.
decision_logic.action: Keep it for at least 2 years from its own date and keep it available for inspection and copying; do not let a newer record retire an older one still inside its period.

decision_logic.condition: A registrant is moving financial and shipping records to a central location.
decision_logic.action: Send the written notification by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, in triplicate, to the Special Agent in Charge, wait the 14 days after receipt before moving anything, and leave executed order forms and the inventories where the regulations require them.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts registrant is adding a principal place of business.
decision_logic.action: Apply for a separate controlled substance registration for that place of business rather than treating the existing registration as covering it, and expect the federal position to be the same, since 21 CFR 1301.12(a) requires a separate DEA registration for each principal place of business.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts inspector asks about an inventory or record failure and the pharmacy answers that the rule is federal.
decision_logic.action: Read M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15: the federal record-keeping and inventory requirements are Massachusetts duties of a registered person, and the Board may add rules of its own for a retail drug business.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts registration term or expiry has to be worked out.
decision_logic.action: Identify the registrant type first. Pharmacy and outsourcing facility registrations run two years from January 1st of an even-numbered year; a wholesale druggist registration runs one year from December 1st.

ma_vs_federal.text: The detailed inventory and retention mechanics in this section are written in federal regulations, but they are not for that reason only federal duties. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires registered persons to keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the federal record-keeping and inventory requirements, so the same failure can be answered for in Massachusetts.

The same statute lets Massachusetts go further, since it adds any additional rules promulgated by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy in the case of a retail drug business. The Schedule II perpetual inventory reconciled at least once every ten days under 247 CMR 9.21(8) is such an addition, and 21 CFR part 1304 states no counterpart to it, so a candidate who reads only the federal inventory rules will miss it.

Being premises-based is common ground rather than a Massachusetts distinction: 21 CFR 1301.12(a) requires a separate DEA registration for each principal place of business and 21 CFR 1304.11(a) a separate inventory for each registered location, while 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate Board controlled substance registration at each principal place of business.

Massachusetts has two controlled substance registers, and 247 CMR 11.00 is only one of them. A pharmacy's controlled substance registration comes from the Board, because M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) excepts a pharmacy, wholesale druggist and outsourcing facility from registering with the commissioner of public health and sends every pharmacy to the Board instead, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) reaches every person other than a registered retail drug business or wholesale druggist. Registrant in 105 CMR 700.000 means a person registered by the Department, so a duty that regulation places on a registrant is not, without more, a duty of a Board-registered pharmacy.

Both bodies of law use a two-year period, but they measure it differently. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) measures two years from the registrant's previous biennial inventory date, while 247 CMR 11.06 measures the pharmacy and outsourcing facility terms from January 1st of an even-numbered year.

The federal biennial interval is uniform across registrants, whereas the Massachusetts term is not: 247 CMR 11.06 gives a wholesale druggist one year from December 1st rather than two years from January 1st.

Federal law states the record-retention floor as at least 2 years from the date of the inventory or record under 21 CFR 1304.04(a); a Massachusetts registration term is not a retention period and does not measure how long any record is kept.

exceptions.text: Commencing business with no controlled substances on hand does not remove the initial-inventory duty. 21 CFR 1304.11(b) has the registrant record that fact as the initial inventory.

The statutory coordination with a regular general physical inventory in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) is not an exception that extends the DEA deadline; the regulation gives effect to it by permitting any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date.

Estimation is itself the exception, and it has a limit. An opened Schedule III, IV or V container may be estimated only where it does not hold more than 1,000 tablets or capsules; above that an exact count is required, and Schedules I and II are outside the estimation rule altogether.

The exception clause opening 21 CFR 1304.04(a) points to paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2), which govern where records may be held rather than how long. Financial and shipping records such as invoices and packing slips may sit at a central location, and executed order forms subject to 21 CFR 1305.17 and 1305.27 are expressly excluded from that permission.

That permission is conditional and delayed. 21 CFR 1304.04(a)(1) requires written notification by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, in triplicate, to the Special Agent in Charge in the registrant's area, and permits central records only commencing 14 days after the Special Agent in Charge receives the notification, and only unless the registrant is informed that permission is denied.

21 CFR 1304.11(a) makes a separate inventory for each registered location the rule and points to the exception in 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(4), and the same paragraph keeps the inventory at the registered location whatever the central-records arrangement for other records.

A registered retail pharmacy that possesses additional registrations for automated dispensing systems at long term care facilities may keep the part 1304 records for those additional registered sites at the retail pharmacy or another approved central location.

The wholesale druggist is the departure from the Massachusetts registration pattern: one year beginning December 1st, against two years beginning January 1st of an even-numbered year for a pharmacy and for an outsourcing facility.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial controlled-substance inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: On the date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances
timing_deadlines.consequence: The inventory is due that day whether or not any controlled substances are on hand; if none are, that fact is recorded as the initial inventory.

timing_deadlines.event: Biennial controlled-substance inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least every two years, on any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date
timing_deadlines.consequence: Once two years have passed from the previous inventory date the registrant is out of compliance, and choosing a later convenient date does not cure it.

timing_deadlines.event: Coordination with a regular general physical inventory under 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The general inventory date nearest to and not varying by more than six months from the biennial date that would otherwise apply
timing_deadlines.consequence: The current regulation gives effect to this by permitting any date within the two-year window; it does not push the deadline past two years.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of an inventory or other part 1304 record
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least 2 years from the date of that inventory or record
timing_deadlines.consequence: The record must be kept by the registrant and available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration throughout the period.

timing_deadlines.event: Start of central recordkeeping for financial and shipping records
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 14 days after the Special Agent in Charge receives the written notification
timing_deadlines.consequence: The notification goes by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, in triplicate, and central records may be kept only from the end of that period and only unless permission is denied.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year
timing_deadlines.consequence: The term is fixed by the calendar, so it runs to the end of the following odd-numbered year regardless of when the registration was issued or when an inventory was taken.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to an outsourcing facility
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year
timing_deadlines.consequence: The outsourcing facility runs on the same cycle as a pharmacy, which is why the wholesale term is the one that has to be memorised separately.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a wholesale druggist
timing_deadlines.timeframe: One year beginning on December 1st of each year
timing_deadlines.consequence: The term is half as long as the pharmacy term and starts on December 1st rather than January 1st, one month before the pharmacy cycle turns over, so a diary built on the pharmacy cycle will be wrong.

forms_records.text: Every inventory is kept in written, typewritten or printed form at the registered location, is separate for each registered location and each independent activity registered, and states whether it was taken as of opening or as of close of business on the inventory date.
The initial inventory is a record in its own right, and where no controlled substances are on hand the record of that fact is what satisfies 21 CFR 1304.11(b).

A dispenser's inventory entry for finished-form stock carries the information 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) requires: the name of the substance, each finished form, the number of units or volume of that form in each commercial container, and the number of such commercial containers.

Damaged, defective or impure substances awaiting disposal, stock held for quality control, and stock maintained for extemporaneous compounding are entered under 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iv) with the name, the total quantity, and the reason the substance is being maintained.

Every inventory and other record required under 21 CFR part 1304 is kept by the registrant and produced for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration for at least 2 years from its date.

A registrant that wishes to keep financial and shipping records centrally under 21 CFR 1304.04(a)(1) notifies the Administration in writing, by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, in triplicate, to the Special Agent in Charge in its area, and the notification states the nature of the records, the exact location where they will be kept, the name, address, DEA registration number and type of registration of the registrant, and whether the records will be in manual or computer readable form; central records may begin 14 days after that notification is received and only unless permission is denied.

The Massachusetts registration is itself a per-premises record: 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business, so an owner with several sites holds several registrations rather than one document listing them.

role_duties.duty: Take an inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand on the date activity first begins, and record a nil position where nothing is on hand.
Take a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years, on a date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date.

Record the container-level information the regulation requires, then make an exact count or measure for opened Schedule I and II containers and an estimate for opened Schedule III to V containers except where more than 1,000 tablets or capsules are held.

Keep it in written, typewritten or printed form at the registered location, transcribe any oral recording promptly, make it separate for each registered location and independent activity, and indicate on it whether it was taken as of opening or close of business.

role_duties.role: Registrant with more than one premises
role_duties.duty: Hold a separate DEA registration for each principal place of business under 21 CFR 1301.12(a) as well as a separate Massachusetts controlled substance registration under 247 CMR 11.05.

Keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the federal requirements as a matter of Massachusetts law, and comply with any additional Board rules applicable to a retail drug business, such as the Schedule II perpetual inventory.
Keep every inventory and other required record for at least 2 years from its date and keep it available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration.
Inspect and copy the registrant's inventories and other part 1304 records, which is the availability the retention paragraph is written to protect.

Hold a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business where it manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances, and track the term that attaches to its own registrant type.

common_traps.text: Waiting for the first shipment before taking the initial inventory, when 21 CFR 1304.11(b) fixes the inventory to the date activity begins and expressly covers the case of commencing business with nothing on hand.
Letting a wholesaler's invoice or a delivery record stand in for the initial inventory, when what the paragraph requires is the registrant's own inventory of stocks on hand.
Treating a zero-stock initial inventory as no inventory, which then moves the start of the biennial cycle forward to the first delivery.

Reading the six-month general-physical-inventory clause in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) as a grace period added to the regulatory deadline, when the regulation implements it as any date inside the same two-year window.
Supposing that only Schedule II stock is inventoried biennially, when 21 CFR 1304.11(c) speaks of all stocks of controlled substances on hand.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Each inventory shall contain a complete and accurate record of all controlled substances on hand on the date the inventory is taken, and shall be maintained in written, typewritten, or printed form at the registered location. An inventory taken by use of an oral recording device must be promptly transcribed. A separate inventory shall be made for each registered location and each independent activity registered, except as provided in 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(4). The inventory may be taken either as of opening of business or as of the close of business on the inventory date, and it shall be indicated on the inventory.

A registrant takes an initial controlled-substance inventory on the date it first engages in controlled-substance activity; if the registrant commences business with no controlled substances on hand, it must record that zero-stock fact as the initial inventory.
exceptions: Starting business with zero controlled substances does not eliminate the initial-inventory record; the registrant records that none are on hand.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: After the initial inventory, a registrant must take a new controlled-substance inventory at least every two years. Current DEA regulation permits any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory; the related statutory general-physical-inventory language does not authorize delaying the DEA inventory beyond that regulatory two-year window.
exceptions: The statutory coordination with a regular general physical inventory does not extend the DEA regulatory deadline past two years from the previous biennial inventory.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Schedule II inventory requires an exact count or measure; Schedule III through V opened containers may generally be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 units.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: DEA-required controlled-substance inventories and records must be maintained and available for inspection for at least two years unless another provision requires longer.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A separate DEA registration is required for each principal place of business or professional practice at one general physical location where controlled substances are manufactured, distributed, imported, exported, or dispensed by a person.

Persons registered to manufacture, distribute, dispense, or possess controlled substances shall keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the record-keeping and inventory requirements of the federal Comprehensive Drug Prevention and Control Act of 1970 or any amendment thereof, and the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, and with any additional rules or regulations promulgated by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy in the case of a retail drug business or wholesale druggist, or by the Commissioner in all other cases.
A Massachusetts pharmacy must maintain controlled substances securely and comply with the storage, access, accountability, and loss-response requirements in 247 CMR 9.21 and applicable federal law.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A SEPARATE controlled substance registration is required at EACH PRINCIPAL PLACE OF BUSINESS where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances. The term differs by registrant: a registration issued to a PHARMACY is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each EVEN-NUMBERED year; a registration issued to an OUTSOURCING FACILITY is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year; and a registration issued to a WHOLESALE DRUGGIST is valid for ONE year beginning DECEMBER 1st of each year.

Registrant, for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.000, means a person who is registered by the Department pursuant to any provision of M.G.L. c. 94C. Under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) every person other than a registered retail drug business or wholesale druggist shall register with the Commissioner where that person manufactures, distributes or dispenses a controlled substance, uses one in research, teaching or chemical analysis, possesses one with intent to do either, or is required to register pursuant to M.G.L. c. 94C; 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3) requires a Health Facility, among other facilities, to register for the purpose of purchase and storage of controlled substances. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) the requirement to register with the commissioner of public health applies except in the case of a pharmacy, wholesale druggist or outsourcing facility, and every pharmacy shall instead register with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy in accordance with its regulations.

full_prose_under_review.title: Securing Controlled Stock, Reporting Theft or Loss, and Disposing of It Lawfully
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Physical and personnel security of the controlled stock, the theft-or-loss report, and the permitted disposal routes with their destruction standard and records
learning_objectives: State what 247 CMR 9.21 requires of a Massachusetts pharmacy: where controlled substances are stored, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, and what the alarm, camera and barrier paragraphs demand.
Say who is responsible for pharmacy security and access to the prescription area, and who may and may not make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory.
Identify who 105 CMR 700.005(B) binds before applying it, and state the federal hiring bar in 21 CFR 1301.76(a) that reaches every DEA-registered pharmacy.
Separate a discrepancy found on a count from a reportable event, and name the two federal clocks that both start at discovery of a theft or significant loss.

List the factors 21 CFR 1301.76(b) tells a registrant to weigh in judging whether a loss is significant, and say which sentences of the non-practitioner paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c) do not travel with it.

Lay the Massachusetts theft and loss routes beside the federal one: the seven-day Board report with a copy of the DEA Form 106 under 247 CMR 20.03(7), the simultaneous police copies under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15, and the 24-hour Drug Control Program report under 105 CMR 700.008.
Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of controlled substances in its own inventory, and identify the route that is written for non-practitioners only.
State the non-retrievable standard in 21 CFR 1317.90 and match each destination in 21 CFR 1317.95 to the two-employee procedure it carries.
Say when a DEA Form 41 is the required record of destruction under 21 CFR 1304.21(e), when it is not, and what separate use 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) makes of the same form.
State the reverse distributor's own registration duty, the delivery controls in 21 CFR 1317.15(b), and the 30-calendar-day destruction deadline in 21 CFR 1317.15(d).
Name the order form and record a Schedule II movement out of the pharmacy carries, whether it goes to a reverse distributor or back for return or recall.

orientation.text: Security in a Massachusetts pharmacy is a list of checkable conditions rather than a general aspiration, and 247 CMR 9.21 states them one at a time. All controlled substances are stored within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V are stored in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion, so dispersal is a third permitted arrangement rather than a relaxation of the first two. The pharmacy maintains a centrally monitored security system that is able to detect a breach in security and is designed to prevent theft, and activates it when the pharmacy is closed. It maintains surveillance cameras in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances, and retains video records for at least 14 days or, in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion, at least two years. A pharmacy located within another retail establishment is secured by a floor to ceiling barrier, securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed. All drug order deliveries containing controlled substances are delivered directly to the pharmacy. None of this switches off for stock the pharmacy no longer wants, because 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Who may be near the stock is settled in several places that answer different questions, and the first thing to settle is which of them is addressed to the pharmacy in front of you. 247 CMR 9.21(6) fixes responsibility inside the pharmacy: the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible for pharmacy security and shall control access to the prescription area. The perpetual-inventory paragraph narrows that further, providing that an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or in the Manager of Record's absence by a pharmacist designee who then reports to the Manager of Record, that an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust the perpetual inventory, and that a certified pharmacy technician may make entries. The hiring question is where a candidate most easily reaches for the wrong sovereign, so read the addressee of each rule before applying it.

105 CMR 700.005(B) is a Department of Public Health rule, and it speaks to applicants and registrants. Registrant is defined in 105 CMR 700.001 as a person who is registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and the Department's own registration provision excludes the retail pharmacy: 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) reaches every person other than a registered retail drug business or wholesale druggist, while M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) requires every pharmacy to register with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy instead. So the personnel provisions of 105 CMR 700.005(B) reach an operator that holds a Department registration, such as a hospital or other health facility registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3), and not a Board-licensed retail pharmacy in that capacity. 247 CMR 9.21(12) shows the same division from the Board's side, sending only an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy to 105 CMR 700.000 for storage and security. What those provisions say, where they apply, is this. All applicants and registrants shall screen before employment new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled. Under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) the screening is made solely for the purpose of determining whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and documentation of the screening is made available to the Commissioner upon request rather than filed in advance. Under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) no registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time.

The hiring rule that does bind every DEA-registered pharmacy is federal. Under 21 CFR 1301.76(a) the registrant shall not employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, any person who has been convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances, or who at any time had an application for registration with DEA denied, had a DEA registration revoked, or has surrendered a DEA registration for cause, which the paragraph defines as a surrender in lieu of or as a consequence of a federal or state administrative, civil or criminal action arising from an investigation of that individual's handling of controlled substances. Compare it with the Department rule rather than merging the two. The federal bar is wider in what it catches, because it adds felony drug convictions and surrenders for cause. It is narrower in who it catches, because it reaches an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, so what the person is actually allowed to touch is part of the federal test in a way it is not part of the Department's. And neither rule is written without any route out: 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive one or more requirements imposed through 105 CMR 700.000 on stated findings, and 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to any provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion.

A missing quantity is not automatically a reportable event, and the sequence matters. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires a pharmacy to reconcile the perpetual inventory for each Schedule II controlled substance at least once every ten days by performing an accurate physical count of inventory on hand and comparing it with the perpetual inventory, and it then puts the next step on one person: the Manager of Record shall investigate any discrepancy and report any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements. The federal requirement for a pharmacy sits in 21 CFR 1301.76(b), the paragraph written for practitioners, because 21 U.S.C. 802(21) names a pharmacy in the definition of practitioner; the parallel paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c) is written for non-practitioners. Under 1301.76(b) the registrant shall notify the Field Division Office of the Administration in its area, in writing, of the theft or significant loss of any controlled substances within one business day of discovery, and must also file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery. Those are two duties running on two clocks, not one duty with a long deadline. Significance is judged rather than counted, against the factors the paragraph supplies: the actual quantity lost in relation to the type of business, the specific substances lost, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, a pattern of losses over a specific time period with whether they appear random and the results of efforts taken to resolve them, and, if known, whether the substances are likely candidates for diversion together with local trends and other indicators of diversion potential.

Two sentences that candidates attach to a pharmacy belong to the non-practitioner paragraph instead, and the difference is worth holding. 21 CFR 1301.74(c) is the paragraph that says expressly that thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties are identified and action taken against them, and it is the paragraph that allocates in-transit losses to the supplier, unless the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction. Neither sentence appears in 21 CFR 1301.76(b). What 1301.76 says about goods in transit runs the other way: under 1301.76(d) a retail pharmacy that contracts with a private, common or contract carrier to retrieve filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy is itself responsible for reporting in-transit losses on a DEA Form 106 upon discovery. 21 CFR 1301.76(c) adds a bridge worth knowing: whenever a practitioner distributes a controlled substance without being registered as a distributor, as 21 CFR 1307.11, 1317.05 and 1317.10 permit, it must comply with the non-practitioner requirements in 21 CFR 1301.74(a), (b) and (e), which is how the carrier-selection duty reaches a pharmacy sending stock out for disposal.

Massachusetts adds two further routes to the federal one, with their own actors and their own clocks, and the DEA filing answers for none of them. First, 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by submitting to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and to comply where applicable with the reporting requirements of the DEA, the Department and the state and local police. Because the Board wants the Form 106 inside seven days, a Massachusetts pharmacy cannot in practice use the whole federal 45. Second, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 attaches copies to that Form 106: a person registered to dispense who discovers a theft or loss requiring the filing of a DEA Form 106 shall simultaneously file a copy with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police, while a person registered to distribute files its copy with the state police. Third, and separately, 105 CMR 700.008 gives a registrant of the Department 24 hours from discovery to report the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department on the form that programme provides or approves. That route binds an operator that holds a Department registration, such as a hospital, and it is what 247 CMR 20.03(7) points a Board-licensed pharmacy at when it says to comply with the Department's requirements where applicable.

Disposal is not ordinary waste handling with extra paperwork. It is a separate scheme with its own part of the regulations, its own permitted destinations and its own witnessing rules, so the answer cannot be reached by asking what is convenient or what the state's waste rules would tolerate. 21 CFR 1317.05(a) opens with a closed list: a registered practitioner in lawful possession of a controlled substance in its inventory that desires to dispose of that substance shall do so in one of the following ways. Those ways are prompt destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317 using an on-site method of destruction; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the registrant's registered location; prompt delivery, for the purpose of return or recall, to the registered person from whom the substance was obtained, to the registered manufacturer of the substance, or to another registrant the manufacturer has authorized to accept returns or recalls on its behalf; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge of the Administration in the area in which the practitioner is located. A retail pharmacy is a practitioner for these purposes, because 21 U.S.C. 802(21) names a pharmacy in the definition of practitioner. The route that lets a registrant carry the substances to the destruction site by its own means is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners, and so is not on the practitioner's list.

Choosing a destination does not dispose of the ordering paperwork, and this is the gap a Schedule II disposal most often leaves. 21 CFR 1305.03 requires either a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent for each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, and its exception for distributions to reverse distributors is written for collectors and law enforcement rather than for a pharmacy emptying its own shelf. So sending expired Schedule II stock to a reverse distributor is a distribution that runs on an order form. The same is true of the return-or-recall route by its own provision: 21 CFR 1317.10(b) requires each registrant that delivers a Schedule I or II controlled substance for the purpose of return or recall to use an order form in the manner described in part 1305, and 21 CFR 1317.10(a) requires a record of each return or recall transaction. On those movements the pharmacy is the party filling the order rather than placing it, so the federal record it keeps is the original of the form under 21 CFR 1305.17(b), maintained separately from all other records for two years, and, because a pharmacy does not report to ARCOS, a copy of that original goes to DEA at the close of the month under 21 CFR 1305.13(d). None of that displaces the Massachusetts record: 247 CMR 9.21(9) still requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II.

Whichever route is chosen, the destruction standard and the record are fixed. 21 CFR 1317.90 requires all controlled substances to be destroyed by a registrant, or caused to be destroyed by a registrant under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), to be destroyed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations and to be rendered non-retrievable. Where multiple controlled substances are comingled the method must be sufficient to render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected for destruction are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient to render non-retrievable any controlled substance likely to be present. Non-retrievable is a defined term for the purposes of the disposal part: the substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means, so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or a controlled substance analogue. 21 CFR 1317.95 then attaches two employees to every destination, and 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record to only two of them: any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d), or causes the destruction of a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), shall maintain a record of destruction on a DEA Form 41 that is complete and accurate and includes the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction. Massachusetts layers its own record on top: 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy runs its ten-day Schedule II reconciliation and finds 40 tablets of one product on hand against a perpetual-inventory balance of 70. A technician offers to correct the record to match the count so that the next reconciliation starts clean, and the pharmacist on duty suggests waiting until month end to see whether the numbers settle before telling anyone.
steps: Separate the count from the conclusion. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires the reconciliation at least once every ten days and then requires the Manager of Record to investigate any discrepancy, so the count triggers an investigation rather than itself establishing a loss.

Fix who may touch the record. 247 CMR 9.21(8) permits an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy to be performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or by a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence who then reports to the Manager of Record, and it bars an unlicensed individual from making any entry into or adjusting the perpetual inventory.

Judge significance against the factors 21 CFR 1301.76(b) supplies rather than against a threshold: the actual quantity in relation to the type of business, the specific substance, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, any pattern over a specific time period with whether the losses appear random and the results of efforts to resolve them, and, if known, the diversion potential of the substance and local trends.

If the investigation establishes a theft or significant loss, start both federal clocks from discovery: written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day, and a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days.

Add the Massachusetts routes rather than stopping at DEA. 247 CMR 20.03(7) gives the pharmacy seven days from the theft or significant loss to submit to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and the DEA Form 106, which in practice pulls the Form 106 well inside the federal 45 days.

Send the police copies with the federal filing. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 a person registered to dispense who must file a DEA Form 106 shall simultaneously file a copy with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police.

Preserve the evidence the state rule expects to exist. 247 CMR 9.21(4) requires video records to be retained for at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected, rather than the ordinary 14 days.
worked_examples.resolution: The Manager of Record investigates, the technician does not adjust the record, and if the investigation establishes a theft or significant loss four things follow from discovery: the one-business-day DEA notice, the Form 106, the Board's seven-day report carrying a copy of that Form 106, and the simultaneous police copies. The error the scenario invites is treating an inventory adjustment as the response to a discrepancy, which destroys the evidence the investigation needs; the second is letting a wait-and-see period run against a clock the regulation starts at discovery rather than at proof; the third is answering the whole question with the DEA filing and leaving the Board and the police unserved.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy has expired Schedule II and Schedule IV stock sitting in a quarantine bin on an open shelf, waiting for the reverse distributor's next pick-up. A technician has already filled out a DEA Form 41 for the bin so the paperwork will be ready, and an intern asks whether the bin still has to sit inside the secured storage now that the drugs can no longer be dispensed.
steps: Name the route. Delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the pharmacy's registered location, is one of the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of inventory.

Check the recipient's status rather than its business description. 21 CFR 1317.15(a) requires any person that reverse distributes a controlled substance to be registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor unless exempted by law or otherwise authorized.

Apply 21 CFR 1317.95 to the hand-over itself. A transfer to a person registered or authorized to accept the substances for destruction falls under paragraph (a), so two employees of the transferring registrant load and unload, or observe the loading and unloading, until the transfer is complete.

Ask what 21 CFR 1304.21(e) actually attaches the Form 41 to. It is the record for a registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c); handing stock to a reverse distributor is neither, so the pharmacy destroys nothing and creates no such record.

Find the record that the Schedule II half of the bin does need. 21 CFR 1305.03 requires a DEA Form 222 or electronic order for each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, and its exception for distributions to reverse distributors is written for collectors and law enforcement, so the Schedule II stock moves on an order form while the Schedule IV stock does not.

Place that form correctly. On this movement the pharmacy fills the order rather than placing it, so it retains the original under 21 CFR 1305.17(b), separately from all other records, and, not reporting to ARCOS, submits a copy to DEA at the close of the month under 21 CFR 1305.13(d).

Answer the intern from 247 CMR 9.21(10), which applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution, so the bin belongs inside the security the section requires.

Note where the duty travels next. 21 CFR 1317.15(d) requires the reverse distributor to destroy or cause the destruction of any controlled substance received for the purpose of destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.
worked_examples.resolution: The bin goes back into secured storage, the Schedule II stock moves on a DEA Form 222 or electronic order whose original the pharmacy keeps, the pick-up follows the two-employee transfer procedure, and the pharmacy records the transfer under 247 CMR 9.21(9) rather than on a Form 41. The error the scenario invites is treating the DEA Form 41 as a receipt for anything that leaves the pharmacy for disposal, when it is a record of destruction; the second is assuming that stock which can no longer be dispensed has passed out of the reach of the security rule; the third is forgetting that a Schedule II hand-over is still a distribution and still needs an order form.

worked_examples.scenario: Two employers in Massachusetts are looking at the same applicant for a stock assistant who will unpack deliveries beside the controlled-substance store. One is a Board-licensed retail Drug Store pharmacy; the other is a hospital that holds a Department of Public Health controlled substance registration. Nine years ago the applicant surrendered his own DEA registration in the face of an investigation into his handling of controlled substances, and he has worked without incident since. Each employer asks whether it may hire him if it documents the history and keeps him away from the controlled-substance store itself.
steps: Take the Department rule first and read its addressee. 105 CMR 700.005(B) binds applicants and registrants, 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) excludes a registered retail drug business from Department registration while M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) sends every pharmacy to the Board instead. The hospital is a Department registrant; the retail pharmacy is not.

Apply the Department provisions to the hospital. It screens before employment, because the applicant may work in or around an area where controlled substances are handled; under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) that screening is made solely to determine whether he is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and the documentation is produced to the Commissioner on request rather than filed in advance. Then read 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2): its two limbs are a denied application and a revoked registration, and a surrender is neither, so this history does not trigger that bar.

Turn to the rule that binds both employers. 21 CFR 1301.76 states security controls for practitioners, and 21 U.S.C. 802(21) makes both a pharmacy and a hospital practitioners, so paragraph (a) reaches each of them as a DEA registrant. It forbids employing, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, anyone who has surrendered a DEA registration for cause, which the paragraph defines as a surrender in lieu of or as a consequence of an action arising from an investigation of that individual's handling of controlled substances.

Notice that access is part of the federal test. The federal bar reaches an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, so unlike the Department's flat prohibition on employing the person, a genuine restriction of access is a question the federal wording puts in play rather than an irrelevance.
Give the time element its weight. The federal registration limbs run at any time, so nine clean years do not lift them, and neither rule offers a look-back period as a route out.

Read the remaining routes before concluding that nothing can be done. 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion, and 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive a requirement of 105 CMR 700.000 for a Department registrant on findings of undue hardship, no jeopardy to health or safety, acceptable compensating measures and written documentation.

Remember that hiring is not the only access control. 247 CMR 9.21(6) makes the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty responsible for pharmacy security and requires them to control access to the prescription area, so even a lawful hire does not arrive with unrestricted access.
worked_examples.resolution: Neither employer may put him in a post with access to controlled substances, and the reason is the federal bar in 21 CFR 1301.76(a) rather than the Department provision: a surrender for cause is one of the federal limbs and is not one of the two limbs in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2). The errors the scenario invites are applying a Department rule to a Board-licensed pharmacy that is not a Department registrant, and treating a restriction of duties as irrelevant when the federal bar is expressly about access.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where does 247 CMR 9.21 require a pharmacy to store controlled substances, and what are the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V go in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long must a Massachusetts pharmacy retain surveillance video records, and what changes the answer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least 14 days, and at least two years in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who is responsible for pharmacy security under 247 CMR 9.21, and who may make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible and control access to the prescription area. A certified pharmacy technician may make entries; an unlicensed individual may not make any entry or adjustment; and an adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the Manager of Record, or by a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence who then reports to the Manager of Record.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who does 105 CMR 700.005(B) bind, and how do you tell?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Applicants and registrants of the Department. 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) excludes a registered retail drug business from that registration, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) sends every pharmacy to the Board instead. A hospital or other health facility registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3) is bound; a Board-licensed retail pharmacy is not, in that capacity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where a 105 CMR 700.005(B) screening is owed, when does it happen, what single purpose does it serve, and where does the documentation go?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Before employment, for new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled; solely to determine whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances; and the documentation is made available to the Commissioner upon request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the employment bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) and the words that decide how long it lasts.
retrieval_prompts.answer: No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time. The closing words at any time leave no look-back period.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the federal hiring bar that reaches every DEA-registered pharmacy, and the three things it adds to or subtracts from the Department's version.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 21 CFR 1301.76(a) a registrant shall not employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause. It adds felony drug convictions and surrenders for cause, and it is confined to employees who have access to controlled substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Two clocks start when a theft or significant loss is discovered at a pharmacy. Name each, and name the provision they come from.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, and a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 filed with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery. Both sit in 21 CFR 1301.76(b), the practitioner paragraph, rather than in 21 CFR 1301.74(c).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two sentences of 21 CFR 1301.74(c) have no counterpart in 21 CFR 1301.76(b)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties identified, and the allocation of in-transit losses to the supplier. 21 CFR 1301.76(d) runs the other way for a retail pharmacy that contracts the carrier retrieving filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Massachusetts Drug Store pharmacy has to file a DEA Form 106. What else is owed, to whom, and on what clock?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and of the DEA Form 106 to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss under 247 CMR 20.03(7), and, simultaneously with the Form 106 filing, a copy to the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and to the department of state police under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which theft or loss route runs on 24 hours, who owes it, and what starts it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 700.008: a registrant of the Department reports theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery, on the form that programme provides or approves. Suspicion of tampering is a trigger in its own right.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy sends expired Schedule II stock to a reverse distributor. Which federal instrument does that movement need, and why is the reverse-distributor exception in 21 CFR 1305.03 no answer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent, because the movement is a distribution of a Schedule II controlled substance. The exception in 21 CFR 1305.03(f) covers distributions to reverse distributors by collectors and law enforcement, not a pharmacy disposing of its own inventory.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 21 CFR 1317.10 require of a registrant that delivers Schedule II stock for return or recall?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An order form used in the manner described in part 1305, and a record of the return or recall transaction; deliveries may go through a freight forwarding facility operated by the person to whom the substance is being returned only on advance notice and with direct delivery to that person's agent or employee.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of a controlled substance in its own inventory.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Prompt on-site destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location; prompt delivery for return or recall to the registered person from whom it was obtained, the registered manufacturer, or another registrant the manufacturer authorized to accept returns or recalls; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge in the practitioner's area, made by submitting one copy of a DEA Form 41 listing the substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does non-retrievable mean, and what does 21 CFR 1317.90 require where substances are comingled or unidentified?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or analogue. Where substances are comingled the method must render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient for any controlled substance likely to be present.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which two paragraphs of 21 CFR 1317.95 make a DEA Form 41 the required record, and what must that record contain?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Paragraph (d), on-site destruction, and paragraph (c), causing destruction after transport to a location that is not registered. Under 21 CFR 1304.21(e) the record must be complete and accurate and include the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How soon must a reverse distributor destroy a controlled substance it received for destruction, and where may a delivery to it be made?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No later than 30 calendar days after receipt. Delivery may be made only to the reverse distributor at its registered location, may not be re-routed to any other location or person once en route regardless of registration status, and must be personally received by an employee of the reverse distributor at the registered location.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which controlled stock does 247 CMR 9.21 stop protecting once it has been set aside for disposal?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None. 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

quick_review.text: A pharmacy stores all controlled substances within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner, and stores Schedules II through V in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances so as to obstruct theft and diversion.
A centrally monitored security system able to detect a breach in security and designed to prevent theft is maintained and activated when the pharmacy is closed.

Surveillance cameras are maintained in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances, and video records are retained at least 14 days, or at least two years in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion.
A pharmacy located within another retail establishment is secured by a floor to ceiling barrier, securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed.
All drug order deliveries containing controlled substances are delivered directly to the pharmacy.
The pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible for pharmacy security and control access to the prescription area.
