The Schedule II perpetual inventory is reconciled at least once every ten days by an accurate physical count compared with the record, and the Manager of Record investigates any discrepancy and reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements.

105 CMR 700.005(B) is addressed to applicants and registrants of the Department; 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) together with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) leaves a retail drug business registered with the Board rather than with the Department.

Where it applies, screening under 105 CMR 700.005(B) happens before employment, reaches new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled, and serves solely to determine whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances.
Documentation of that screening is made available to the Commissioner upon request, which is a duty to produce rather than a duty to file.

No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time.

21 CFR 1301.76(a) forbids a registrant to employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause.
A pharmacy is a practitioner under 21 U.S.C. 802(21), which is why its federal security duties sit in 21 CFR 1301.76 rather than in the non-practitioner section 21 CFR 1301.74.

Written notice of the theft or significant loss of any controlled substances goes to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, under 21 CFR 1301.76(b).
A complete and accurate DEA Form 106 is filed with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery of the theft or loss.

Significance is judged against the quantity lost in relation to the type of business, the specific substances lost, association with access by specific individuals or with unique activities, any pattern of losses over a specific time period with whether they appear random and the results of efforts to resolve them, and, if known, diversion candidacy and local trends.

247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to submit to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of a theft or significant loss of controlled substances.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires a person registered to dispense who must file a DEA Form 106 to file a copy simultaneously with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police; a person registered to distribute files with the state police.

105 CMR 700.008 gives a registrant of the Department 24 hours from discovery to report theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program on the form that programme provides or approves.

A distribution of Schedule I or II stock out of the pharmacy, including a delivery to a reverse distributor, requires a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent, because the 21 CFR 1305.03 exception for distributions to reverse distributors is written for collectors and law enforcement.
21 CFR 1317.10 requires an order form for a Schedule I or II delivery made for the purpose of return or recall, and a record of each return or recall transaction.

21 CFR 1317.05(a) states a closed list of the ways a practitioner may dispose of a controlled substance in its inventory: prompt on-site destruction, prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, prompt delivery for return or recall, or a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge.

Any person that reverse distributes a controlled substance must be registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor unless exempted by law or otherwise authorized, and 21 CFR 1317.15(d) requires it to destroy or cause the destruction of substances received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

Deliveries to a reverse distributor may be made only at its registered location, may not be re-routed once en route regardless of registration status, and must be personally received by an employee of the reverse distributor at that location.

All controlled substances destroyed by a registrant, or caused to be destroyed under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), must be destroyed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations and rendered non-retrievable.

Where multiple controlled substances are comingled the method must render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient for any controlled substance likely to be present.
21 CFR 1317.95 requires two employees at every destination, and adds the personal witnessing requirement for destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

A registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d), or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), maintains a record of destruction on a DEA Form 41 that is complete and accurate and includes the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

247 CMR 9.21(9) requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

decision_logic.condition: Controlled stock is being put away, locked up or left overnight in a Massachusetts pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.21 paragraph by paragraph: the secured prescription area, one of the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, the centrally monitored system activated at closing, cameras with the retention the section sets, and, inside another retail establishment, the floor to ceiling barrier securely locked and separately alarmed.

decision_logic.condition: A new employee will have access to controlled substances at a DEA-registered pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply 21 CFR 1301.76(a): do not employ, in a post with access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause.

decision_logic.condition: Someone proposes to apply 105 CMR 700.005(B) to an employer.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether that employer is a registrant of the Department. A hospital or other health facility registered under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3) is; a retail drug business licensed and registered by the Board is not, and is reached instead by the federal bar and by the Board's own rules.

decision_logic.condition: A Department registrant is hiring a new employee who may work in or around an area where controlled substances are handled.
decision_logic.action: Screen before employment for trustworthiness around controlled substances, keep the documentation available for the Commissioner on request, and check 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) before extending an offer, because a denied application or a revoked registration for violation of any law or regulation bars knowing employment at any time.

decision_logic.condition: A bar appears to leave no room and someone asks whether there is any route out.
decision_logic.action: Name the two that exist: 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion, and 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive a requirement of 105 CMR 700.000 for a registrant on the four findings it lists. Neither is a right to relief.

decision_logic.condition: A ten-day Schedule II reconciliation, or any other count, produces a discrepancy.
decision_logic.action: Have the Manager of Record investigate before anyone adjusts the record, and let only the Manager of Record, or a pharmacist designee in the Manager of Record's absence, make an adjustment arising from that discrepancy.

decision_logic.condition: The investigation establishes a theft or significant loss of controlled substances.
decision_logic.action: Send written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area within one business day of discovery, and file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery; later recovery of the substances does not lift the duty.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy establishing that theft or significant loss is located in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Run the state routes alongside the federal one: submit a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and the DEA Form 106 to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, which means the Form 106 has to be completed well inside the federal period, and file a copy of that Form 106 simultaneously with the local police department and the department of state police.

decision_logic.condition: The operator discovering the theft, loss or suspected tampering holds a Department of Public Health controlled substance registration, such as a hospital.
decision_logic.action: Add the 24-hour report to the Drug Control Program within the Department on its own form, measured from discovery, and remember that suspected tampering triggers it without any confirmed shortfall.

decision_logic.condition: Schedule I or II stock is leaving the pharmacy for a reverse distributor, a return or a recall.
decision_logic.action: Put the movement on a DEA Form 222 or electronic order, keep the original of the form the pharmacy filled and the record 21 CFR 1317.10(a) requires for a return or recall, and keep the Massachusetts record 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires as well.

decision_logic.condition: Stock is expired, quarantined or otherwise unwanted and has to leave the pharmacy's usable inventory.
decision_logic.action: Pick one of the routes 21 CFR 1317.05(a) lists for a practitioner and act promptly; do not invent a route, and do not treat transport by the pharmacy's own means to a destruction site as one of them.

decision_logic.condition: A vendor offers to collect unwanted controlled stock for disposal.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the vendor is registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor, deliver only to its registered location by an authorized pick-up or carrier, and expect it to destroy or cause the destruction of the substances no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy itself will destroy controlled substances rather than transfer them.
decision_logic.action: Render them non-retrievable in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations, and run the two-employee procedure 21 CFR 1317.95 attaches to the destination, including personal witnessing of the destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

decision_logic.condition: The destruction or the transfer is finished and someone asks which record to create.
decision_logic.action: Create a DEA Form 41 only where 21 CFR 1304.21(e) requires it, namely destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causing destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), and in either case record the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

decision_logic.condition: The stock being disposed of includes Schedule II product, and the pharmacy is in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Keep the accurate record 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including the proper DEA forms for Schedule II, and keep the stock inside the section's security until it leaves.

ma_vs_federal.text: The Massachusetts storage rule is written for a pharmacy and is more specific than a general security duty: 247 CMR 9.21 names the secured prescription area, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, a centrally monitored system activated at closing, cameras with a defined retention period, and a floor to ceiling barrier for a pharmacy inside another retail establishment.

The federal theft-or-loss duty runs to the Administration under 21 CFR 1301.76(b), and 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) routes the same event through the Manager of Record, who investigates any discrepancy and reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements. The state requirements that sentence points at are real ones of their own, not merely a reference back to the federal rule.

Three Massachusetts routes sit alongside the federal filing, and each has its own actor and clock: the Board report within seven days of the theft or significant loss carrying a copy of the DEA Form 106 under 247 CMR 20.03(7), the simultaneous police copies under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15, and the Department's 24-hour report to the Drug Control Program under 105 CMR 700.008, which binds an operator holding a Department registration.

The seven-day Board report is the practical constraint on the federal 45-day period, because 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires the copy of the DEA Form 106 to reach the Board within seven days, so a Massachusetts pharmacy cannot use the whole federal window.

The two hiring bars come from different sovereigns and different registers. 21 CFR 1301.76(a) binds every DEA registrant but only as to employees with access to controlled substances, while 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) binds registrants of the Department and reaches employment as such.

Disposal records stack rather than substitute. The federal record of destruction is the DEA Form 41 required by 21 CFR 1304.21(e), while 247 CMR 9.21(9) separately requires an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

The statute behind that stacking is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15, whose first paragraph requires registered persons to keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the federal record-keeping and inventory requirements and with any additional rules the Board promulgates for a retail drug business. It is the same section whose second paragraph attaches the police copies to a DEA Form 106, so one provision supplies both the Board's power to add a record like 247 CMR 9.21(9) and the police leg of a theft or loss response.

Federal law decides where unwanted stock may go, and Massachusetts decides how it is held until it goes: 21 CFR 1317.05(a) fixes the practitioner's routes, while 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies every security requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

The Massachusetts personnel bar is a state-law hiring prohibition addressed to registrants of the Department under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2). The separate duty in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) to make screening documentation available to the Commissioner on request is a production duty rather than an advance filing, and the regulation does not make it the mechanism by which the bar itself is enforced.

Disposal paperwork stacks across sovereigns too: the federal side supplies the order form for a Schedule II movement and, where destruction occurs, the DEA Form 41, while 247 CMR 9.21(9) adds the Massachusetts record of everything returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of.

exceptions.text: 247 CMR 9.21(11) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.21 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies.
247 CMR 9.21(12) sends an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy to a different source, requiring it to store and secure controlled substances in accordance with 105 CMR 700.000.

Dispersal is the alternative built into 247 CMR 9.21(2): Schedules II through V need not sit in a cabinet if they are dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion.

105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) states no look-back period and no cure of its own, but it is not beyond reach: 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive one or more requirements imposed through 105 CMR 700.000 on findings of undue hardship, no jeopardy to health or safety, compensating measures acceptable to the Commissioner, and written documentation from the registrant.

The federal bar in 21 CFR 1301.76(a) likewise states no exception in its own words, but 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person apply in writing to DEA for an exception to any provision of the chapter, which the Administrator may grant in his discretion and is never required to grant.

The allocation of in-transit losses to the supplier belongs to the non-practitioner paragraph 21 CFR 1301.74(c), and does not travel to a pharmacy under 21 CFR 1301.76. For a practitioner the allocation runs the other way in one case: under 21 CFR 1301.76(d) a retail pharmacy that contracts a carrier to retrieve filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy reports the in-transit loss itself on a DEA Form 106.

The seven-day Board theft or loss report carries its own limits in its own words: 247 CMR 20.03(7) names a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy and nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts, and asks for compliance with the DEA, Department and state and local police requirements only where applicable.

21 CFR 1304.21(e) carves out one destruction from the Form 41 requirement: a controlled substance dispensed by a practitioner for immediate administration at the practitioner's registered location that is not fully exhausted is recorded under the ordinary dispensing-record provision instead.

21 CFR 1317.05(a)(5) allows a standing arrangement where a practitioner is required regularly to dispose of controlled substances: the Special Agent in Charge may authorize disposal without a prior application in each instance, on the condition that the practitioner keeps records of the disposals and files periodic reports summarising them, and may attach further conditions.

timing_deadlines.event: Written notice of a theft or significant loss of controlled substances
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within one business day of discovery of the theft or loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: Notice goes in writing to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area under 21 CFR 1301.76(b), and the duty does not wait for the investigation to finish.

timing_deadlines.event: Filing the DEA Form 106 for that theft or loss
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 45 days after discovery
timing_deadlines.consequence: A complete and accurate Form 106 is filed with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application; this is a second duty, not an extension of the first.

timing_deadlines.event: Board report of a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by a Massachusetts pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within seven days of such theft or significant loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: A copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and of the DEA Form 106 goes to the Board, which means the Form 106 has to be produced well inside the federal 45 days.

timing_deadlines.event: Police copies of a DEA Form 106 filed by a person registered to dispense
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Simultaneously with the filing of the DEA Form 106
timing_deadlines.consequence: A copy goes to the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and to the department of state police, so the copies have no clock independent of the federal filing.

timing_deadlines.event: Department report of theft, loss or suspected tampering by a registrant of the Department
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 24 hours of discovery
timing_deadlines.consequence: The report goes to the Drug Control Program within the Department on the form it provides or approves, and suspected tampering starts the period without any confirmed shortfall.

timing_deadlines.event: Reporting an in-transit loss of filled prescriptions retrieved from a central fill pharmacy under a carrier contracted by the retail pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Upon discovery of the loss
timing_deadlines.consequence: The retail pharmacy reports it by use of a DEA Form 106 under 21 CFR 1301.76(d); the supplier allocation in 21 CFR 1301.74(c) is the non-practitioner rule and does not put this duty elsewhere.

timing_deadlines.event: Reconciling the Schedule II perpetual inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least once every ten days
timing_deadlines.consequence: An accurate physical count of inventory on hand is compared with the perpetual inventory, and any discrepancy goes to the Manager of Record to investigate.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of surveillance video records
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least 14 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: Ordinary retention for cameras maintained in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of surveillance video where theft or diversion is known or suspected
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least two years
timing_deadlines.consequence: The longer period attaches to the same recordings once theft or diversion is known or suspected, so a decision to delete on the ordinary schedule can destroy the evidence the state rule expects to survive.

timing_deadlines.event: Activation of the pharmacy's centrally monitored security system
timing_deadlines.timeframe: When the pharmacy is closed
timing_deadlines.consequence: A pharmacy inside another retail establishment must in addition be securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed.

timing_deadlines.event: Screening a prospective employee who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Before employment
timing_deadlines.consequence: The screening is a condition of hiring rather than an onboarding step, and its documentation must be available to the Commissioner upon request.

timing_deadlines.event: Duration of the bar on knowingly employing a person whose application was denied or whose registration was revoked for violation of any law or regulation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At any time, with no look-back period
timing_deadlines.consequence: The passage of incident-free years does not lift the bar, and no documentation, restriction of duties or notification is offered as a substitute.

timing_deadlines.event: Destruction by a reverse distributor of substances received for the purpose of destruction
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 30 calendar days after receipt
timing_deadlines.consequence: The reverse distributor destroys or causes the destruction of the substances within that period, having stored them under the security controls in parts 1301 and 1317 in the meantime.

timing_deadlines.event: Acting on a decision to dispose of controlled substances in a practitioner's inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Promptly, in the terms 21 CFR 1317.05(a) uses for each route
timing_deadlines.consequence: Destruction, delivery to a reverse distributor and delivery for return or recall are each required to be prompt, so unwanted stock is not left to accumulate under the security rules indefinitely.

forms_records.text: DEA Form 106 is the theft-or-loss filing: complete and accurate, submitted to the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery, and preceded by written notice to the Field Division Office within one business day.

The one-business-day notice is itself a written record, addressed to the Field Division Office of the Administration in the registrant's area; it is the federal leg of the response, and the Massachusetts reports are separate instruments sent elsewhere.

The same DEA Form 106 does double duty in Massachusetts: a copy goes to the Board with the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and a copy goes simultaneously to the local police department and the department of state police.

The Department's route has its own instrument: the form the Drug Control Program provides or approves, submitted within 24 hours of discovery, so a copy of the DEA Form 106 is not what that regulation asks for.

A Schedule I or II movement out of the pharmacy for disposal, return or recall runs on a DEA Form 222 or electronic order, and the pharmacy, as the party filling that order, retains the original under 21 CFR 1305.17(b) and submits a copy to DEA at the close of the month under 21 CFR 1305.13(d).

DEA Form 41 is the record of destruction required by 21 CFR 1304.21(e) from any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) or causes destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c); it must be complete and accurate and include the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction.

A DEA Form 41 is not the record for handing stock to a reverse distributor or for transporting it to a registered location, because 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record only to the two destruction paragraphs of 21 CFR 1317.95.

The same form has a second and different use: 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) has a practitioner submit one copy of a DEA Form 41 to the Special Agent in Charge, listing the controlled substances it desires to dispose of, in order to request disposal assistance.

Where the Special Agent in Charge authorises a practitioner that regularly disposes of controlled substances to act without a prior application in each instance, the practitioner keeps records of those disposals and files periodic reports summarising them.

247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.

The Schedule II perpetual inventory is itself a security record: it may be kept in hard copy or electronically, must reflect the amount of each Schedule II controlled substance located on the pharmacy premises, and covers each such substance the pharmacy has received, dispensed, or disposed of.

That record must include the name and strength of each Schedule II controlled substance, the quantity of each drug purchased or added to inventory, the starting inventory, prescription numbers, the dispensed quantity, the remaining balance, and pharmacist identification for each transaction.
Surveillance video is a record with its own retention rule, kept at least 14 days and at least two years where theft or diversion is known or suspected.
Documentation of pre-employment screening is retained so that it can be made available by applicants and registrants of the Department to the Commissioner upon request.

role_duties.duty: Is responsible for pharmacy security together with the pharmacist on duty, controls access to the prescription area, investigates any discrepancy found on the Schedule II reconciliation, reports any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements, and performs any inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy, which only a pharmacist designee acting in the Manager of Record's absence may perform instead.
May make an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy in the Manager of Record's absence, and then reports the change to the Manager of Record.
May make entries into the Schedule II perpetual inventory, while an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust it.

role_duties.role: Applicant or registrant of the Department as employer
role_duties.duty: Screens new employees before employment where they may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled, keeps the documentation available to the Commissioner on request, and does not knowingly employ any agent or employee barred by 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2).

Does not employ, as an agent or employee with access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who at any time had a DEA application denied, a DEA registration revoked, or a DEA registration surrendered for cause.

Gives written notice to the Field Division Office of the Administration in its area within one business day of discovery and files a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 within 45 days, under 21 CFR 1301.76(b).

role_duties.role: Massachusetts pharmacy that has filed a DEA Form 106
role_duties.duty: Submits a copy of that form with the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and files a copy simultaneously with the local police department and the department of state police.

role_duties.role: Registrant of the Department discovering theft, loss or suspected tampering
role_duties.duty: Reports to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery on the form that programme provides or approves.

role_duties.role: Retail pharmacy that contracted the carrier retrieving filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Reports in-transit losses itself on a DEA Form 106 upon discovery, under 21 CFR 1301.76(d).

role_duties.role: Supplier of a shipment lost in transit under the non-practitioner rule
role_duties.duty: Reports an in-transit loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected within one business day of discovery, except where the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction; this is 21 CFR 1301.74(c) and it is not the rule that governs a pharmacy's own losses.

role_duties.role: The two employees required at a destruction or transfer
role_duties.duty: Load and unload or observe the loading and unloading until a transfer is complete, accompany the substances where the registrant transports them, handle or observe the handling until the substance is rendered non-retrievable, and personally witness the destruction where 21 CFR 1317.95(c) or (d) applies.

Holds its own registration with the Administration, accepts delivery only at its registered location with personal receipt by an employee and no re-routing once en route, stores the substances under the security controls in parts 1301 and 1317, and destroys or causes the destruction of substances received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

role_duties.role: Registrant that destroyed or caused destruction
role_duties.duty: Maintains the DEA Form 41 record of destruction, complete and accurate, with the name and signature of the two witnessing employees.

common_traps.text: Adjusting the perpetual inventory to match a count, which resolves the paperwork and destroys the evidence; 247 CMR 9.21(8) sends a discrepancy to the Manager of Record to investigate and restricts who may make the adjustment at all.
Collapsing the two federal clocks into one, so the written notice waits for the Form 106; the notice is due within one business day of discovery and the Form 106 within 45 days after it.

Answering a Massachusetts theft or loss with the DEA filing alone, when the Board wants a copy of the Form 106 within seven days and the local and state police want copies at the moment the Form 106 is filed.
Treating the federal 45 days as the operative outer limit in Massachusetts, when the seven-day Board report requires the Form 106 much earlier.

Sending the Department's 24-hour report to the Board, or the Board's seven-day report to the Drug Control Program, when the two routes have different recipients, different instruments and different clocks.

Reading a pharmacy's federal theft-or-loss duty out of 21 CFR 1301.74(c), the non-practitioner paragraph, when 21 U.S.C. 802(21) makes a pharmacy a practitioner and 21 CFR 1301.76(b) is its paragraph; the clocks match but the sentences about recovery and in-transit losses do not travel.

Looking for a numerical threshold of significance instead of applying the factors the regulation actually lists, among them quantity in relation to the type of business, association with access by specific individuals, and any pattern of losses over a specific time period.

Reading the theft-or-loss duty in this section as covering anything other than controlled substances; the theft or loss of DEA order forms is a separate duty that belongs with the ordering rules and is not reached here.

Treating a DEA Form 41 as the receipt for anything leaving the pharmacy for disposal, when 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches it to destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(d) and to causing destruction under 21 CFR 1317.95(c) and to nothing else.

Forgetting that the same form appears twice for different reasons, once as the record of a destruction and once as the copy a practitioner submits to the Special Agent in Charge to request disposal assistance.
Assuming a pharmacy may drive unwanted stock to an incinerator itself, when transport by the registrant's own means to a destruction location is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners.
Accepting a disposal vendor on the strength of its business description or a state permit rather than confirming that it is registered with the Administration as a reverse distributor.

Believing that removing labels, crushing tablets or mixing stock into ordinary waste satisfies the destruction standard, when the substance must be rendered non-retrievable by a permanent and irreversible alteration of its physical or chemical condition.

Skipping the second employee, or having one person witness while the other only signs afterwards, when 21 CFR 1317.95 requires two employees at each stage and personal witnessing of the destruction under paragraphs (c) and (d).

Moving expired or quarantined stock out of secured storage because it can no longer be dispensed, when 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies every requirement of the section to substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Reading the screening duty in 105 CMR 700.005(B) as an ordinary background check, when the regulation states that it is made solely to determine whether the prospective employee can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances.
Importing a look-back period into 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2), or answering it with a documented history or a notification, when its two limbs run at any time and neither device appears in the paragraph.
Applying 105 CMR 700.005(B) to a Board-licensed retail pharmacy, when it is addressed to applicants and registrants of the Department and a retail drug business registers with the Board instead.

Missing the federal bar that does reach the pharmacy, and with it the felony drug conviction and surrender-for-cause limbs, or forgetting that the federal bar turns on access to controlled substances so that the scope of a post is part of the test.

Saying that a rule stating no exception of its own admits of none, when 105 CMR 700.140 gives the Commissioner a waiver over 105 CMR 700.000 and 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person ask DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter.

Sending Schedule II stock to a reverse distributor with no order form, on the strength of the 21 CFR 1305.03 exception for distributions to reverse distributors, which is written for collectors and law enforcement.

Forgetting that a Schedule II return or recall has its own instrument and record under 21 CFR 1317.10, and that the pharmacy keeps the original of the order it filled and sends DEA a copy at the close of the month.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Massachusetts pharmacy must maintain controlled substances securely and comply with the storage, access, accountability, and loss-response requirements in 247 CMR 9.21 and applicable federal law.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: All applicants and registrants shall SCREEN BEFORE EMPLOYING new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled. The screening is made SOLELY to determine whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and documentation of it shall be made available to the Commissioner ON REQUEST. NO REGISTRANT SHALL KNOWINGLY EMPLOY any agent or employee who has had an application for registration DENIED for violation of any law or regulation, or has had their registration REVOKED for violation of any law or regulation, AT ANY TIME.

Registrant, for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.000, means a person who is registered by the Department pursuant to any provision of M.G.L. c. 94C. Under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) every person other than a registered retail drug business or wholesale druggist shall register with the Commissioner where that person manufactures, distributes or dispenses a controlled substance, uses one in research, teaching or chemical analysis, possesses one with intent to do either, or is required to register pursuant to M.G.L. c. 94C; 105 CMR 700.004(A)(3) requires a Health Facility, among other facilities, to register for the purpose of purchase and storage of controlled substances. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) the requirement to register with the commissioner of public health applies except in the case of a pharmacy, wholesale druggist or outsourcing facility, and every pharmacy shall instead register with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy in accordance with its regulations.

authority.name: Waiver of requirements imposed on registrants

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The Commissioner may issue a waiver of one or more of the requirements imposed through 105 CMR 700.000 upon a finding that compliance would cause undue hardship to the registrant; that the registrant's noncompliance does not jeopardize the health or safety of individuals or the public; that the registrant has instituted compensating measures that are acceptable to the Commissioner; and that the registrant provides to the Commissioner, or their designee, written documentation supporting its request for a waiver.

A Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy, and nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts shall report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by submitting to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of such theft or significant loss and, where applicable, shall comply with the reporting requirements of the DEA, the Department and the state and local police.

If a person registered to distribute controlled substances discovers a theft or loss of controlled substances that requires the filing of DEA Form 106 with the United States Drug Enforcement Administration, the person shall simultaneously file a copy of that form with the department of state police. If a person registered to dispense controlled substances discovers such a theft or loss, the person shall simultaneously file a copy of that form with the police department in the city or town wherein the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A registrant shall report the THEFT, LOSS OR SUSPECTED TAMPERING of any controlled substances to the DRUG CONTROL PROGRAM within the Department WITHIN 24 HOURS OF DISCOVERY of such theft, loss or suspected tampering, by completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for that purpose.

Persons registered to manufacture, distribute, dispense, or possess controlled substances shall keep records and maintain inventories in conformance with the record-keeping and inventory requirements of the federal Comprehensive Drug Prevention and Control Act of 1970 or any amendment thereof, and the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, and with any additional rules or regulations promulgated by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy in the case of a retail drug business or wholesale druggist, or by the Commissioner in all other cases.

The term practitioner means a physician, dentist, veterinarian, scientific investigator, pharmacy, hospital, or other person licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices or does research, to distribute, dispense, conduct research with respect to, administer, or use in teaching or chemical analysis, a controlled substance in the course of professional practice or research.

The registrant shall notify the Field Division Office of the Administration in his area, in writing, of the theft or significant loss of any controlled substances within one business day of discovery of such loss or theft, and must also file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery of the theft or loss. In determining whether a loss is significant a registrant should consider, among others, the actual quantity lost in relation to the type of business; the specific controlled substances lost; whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities; a pattern of losses over a specific time period, whether the losses appear random, and the results of efforts taken to resolve them; and, if known, whether the substances are likely candidates for diversion and local trends and other indicators of diversion potential. Where a retail pharmacy contracts with private, common or contract carriers to retrieve filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy, the retail pharmacy is responsible for reporting in-transit losses upon discovery by use of a DEA Form 106.

The registrant shall not employ, as an agent or employee who has access to controlled substances, any person who has been convicted of a felony offense relating to controlled substances or who, at any time, had an application for registration with the DEA denied, had a DEA registration revoked or has surrendered a DEA registration for cause. For purposes of that provision, for cause means a surrender in lieu of, or as a consequence of, any federal or state administrative, civil or criminal action resulting from an investigation of the individual's handling of controlled substances.

Any person may apply for an exception to the application of any provision of 21 CFR chapter II by filing a written request with the Office of Diversion Control, Drug Enforcement Administration, stating the reasons for the exception. The Administrator may grant an exception in his discretion, but in no case shall he or she be required to grant an exception to any person which is otherwise required by law or the regulations cited in that section.

authority.name: Federal reporting of significant controlled-substance theft or loss

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A DEA registrant must notify the responsible DEA field division in writing within one business day after discovering a theft or significant loss and complete the required electronic DEA Form 106 process.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Controlled substances destroyed by a registrant must be rendered non-retrievable so their physical or chemical condition is permanently altered and unavailable for practical use.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A registrant that destroys or causes destruction of controlled substances must maintain the required destruction record, generally using DEA Form 41, with the required substance, method, place, date, and witness information.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Schedule I and II ordering by Form 222 or CSOS

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A distribution of Schedule I or II controlled substances generally requires a DEA Form 222 or a compliant digitally signed electronic order unless a listed exception applies.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The supplier must retain the original DEA Form 222 that it has filled, in accordance with 21 CFR 1305.17(c). A supplier that is not required to report acquisition and disposition transactions to ARCOS under 21 CFR 1304.33(c), such as a practitioner, must make and submit a copy of the original DEA Form 222 to DEA, either by mail to the Registration Section or by email to the address the regulation gives; the copy must be forwarded at the close of the month during which the order is filled, or, where an order is filled by partial shipments, at the close of the month during which the final shipment is made or the 60-day validity period expires.

Each registrant shall maintain a record of each return or recall transaction in accordance with the information required of manufacturers in 21 CFR 1304.22(a)(2)(iv). Each registrant that delivers a controlled substance in Schedule I or II for the purpose of return or recall shall use an order form in the manner described in 21 CFR part 1305. Deliveries for the purpose of return or recall may be made through a freight forwarding facility operated by the person to whom the controlled substance is being returned, provided that advance notice of the return is given and delivery is directly to an agent or employee of that person.

authority.name: Transfer to a registered reverse distributor

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A registrant may transfer controlled substances to a DEA-registered reverse distributor under the applicable inventory, ordering, transfer, and record requirements.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

full_prose_under_review.title: Quality-related Events and the Reports They Trigger
full_prose_under_review.topic: Quality assurance and mandatory reporting / Sorting a quality-related event into the right track
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: The CQI Program and its six minimum provisions in 247 CMR 15.02(1), the discovery, notification, 24-hour documentation and analysis sequence in 247 CMR 15.03, the CQI records and two-year QRE retention in 247 CMR 15.04, the seven-business-day serious-event reports and five-year records in 247 CMR 20.02 with the non-resident carve-out and its replacement duty, and the Massachusetts theft or loss reports to the Board and to the Drug Control Program
learning_objectives: List the six minimum provisions a CQI Program shall include under 247 CMR 15.02(1) and identify which of them a bare incident log leaves undone.
Separate the escalation duty that 247 CMR 15.03(1) places on all pharmacy personnel from the three-part immediate response it places on the pharmacist.
State the 24-hour QRE documentation deadline, name what starts it, and reproduce the four content elements required by 247 CMR 15.03(2)(b).
Distinguish the analysis half of 247 CMR 15.03(3) from its response half, and say what each one requires.
Apply the seven-business-day period in 247 CMR 20.02(1) and explain why it runs from discovery of the serious injury or death rather than from the dispensing.
Contrast 247 CMR 20.02(1) with 247 CMR 20.02(2) on the event, the recipients and the trigger that starts the clock.
Explain why a complete QRE record never discharges a Board report, using the words of 247 CMR 20.02(3).
Measure the five-year serious-event retention from the correct date and state the readily retrievable standard that accompanies it.
State the two-year QRE retention in 247 CMR 15.04(2), the date it runs from, and the other records 247 CMR 15.04 requires, and keep it apart from the five-year serious-event period.
Apply the non-resident carve-out in 247 CMR 20.02(5) and the different duty and trigger that 247 CMR 20.07(3) puts in its place.
Route a theft, loss or suspected tampering of controlled substances to every recipient Massachusetts names, on the correct instrument and within the correct period, measured from discovery.
Sort a single set of facts into the CQI track, the Board reporting track, the Drug Control Program track, or more than one of them at once.

orientation.text: 247 CMR 15.02(1) requires each pharmacy to establish a Continuous Quality Improvement Program, and it states the purpose of that programme in four verbs: detecting, documenting, assessing and preventing Quality Related Events. The regulation then fixes a floor beneath the programme. At a minimum a CQI Program shall include provisions to designate an individual or individuals responsible for monitoring CQI Program compliance with the requirements of 247 CMR 15.00, to identify and document QREs, to minimise the impact of QREs on patients, to analyse data collected in response to QREs to assess causes and any contributing factors, to use the findings of that analysis to formulate an appropriate response and develop pharmacy systems and workflow processes designed to prevent QREs, and to provide ongoing education at least annually in the area of CQI to pharmacy personnel. Six provisions, not one. A pharmacy that keeps an incident log and does nothing else has satisfied the second of them and left the other five undone.

The programme is a standing structure. 247 CMR 15.03 is what happens when an event actually occurs, and its first subsection carries two duties that are easy to read as one. All pharmacy personnel shall be trained to bring any QRE to the attention of the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record immediately upon discovery, so the escalation duty reaches the whole staff rather than pharmacists alone. The pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of a QRE shall then immediately provide notification to the patient or the patient's representative, the prescriber if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist, and other members of the healthcare team; directions for correcting the error; and instructions for minimising the negative impact on the patient. Three things are owed rather than one, and the regulation prescribes no sequence among them. The professional-judgment qualifier is the single discretionary element in the subsection, and it attaches to the prescriber notification alone. Notification of the patient or the patient's representative is not conditioned on it.

247 CMR 15.03(2) puts a clock on the paperwork and then says what the paperwork must contain. A QRE shall be initially documented by the pharmacist who has discovered or been informed of it within 24 hours after the QRE is discovered by or described to the pharmacist. Two features of that deadline decide questions. The period is 24 hours and not one business day, so it runs across nights, weekends and holidays. And it starts at discovery or description, so it does not wait for the patient to confirm harm and it is not measured from the dispensing that went wrong. The documentation itself must describe the event sufficiently to permit categorisation and analysis of it, and must include the date when the pharmacist discovered or received notification of the QRE together with the name of the person who notified the pharmacy, the names and titles of the persons recording the QRE information and performing the QRE analysis, a description of the QRE reviewed, and documentation of the contact with the patient or the patient's representative, the prescribing practitioner if indicated in the professional judgment of the pharmacist, and other members of the healthcare team.

247 CMR 15.03(3) closes the loop, and its two halves are separately examinable. Under the analysis half, the investigative and other pertinent data collected in response to QREs shall be analysed, individually and collectively, to assess the cause and any contributing factors such as system or process failures. The analysis and assessment shall include a consideration of the effects on quality assurance related to workflow processes, technological support, personnel training and staffing levels; any recommended remedial changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes; and the development of indicators that identify means against which a pharmacy's program intends to measure its standards over a designated period of time. Under the response half, each pharmacy shall inform pharmacy personnel of changes to pharmacy policies, procedures, systems or processes resulting from recommendations generated by the CQI Program. An analysis whose conclusions never reach the staff who do the work leaves the second half undone, however thorough the first half was.

247 CMR 15.04 closes the CQI regulation with the records it leaves behind, and it answers the retention question a candidate is most likely to ask. Each pharmacy shall maintain a written copy of its CQI Program description on the pharmacy premises, and that description shall be readily available to all pharmacy personnel, so the programme is a document on site rather than a set of habits. Each pharmacy shall maintain a record of all QREs for a minimum period of two years from the date of the QRE report. Read the start point carefully, because it is the date of the QRE report and not the date of the event, the date of the dispensing or the date any Board report was filed. QRE records shall be maintained in an orderly manner and filed by date, which is a condition on how they are kept rather than on how long. And QRE records may be stored at a site other than the pharmacy where the QRE occurred, so an off-site archive is permitted even though the written CQI Program description must be on the premises.

Everything to this point stays inside the pharmacy. 247 CMR 20.02 is where an event leaves the building, and it describes two reports rather than one. Under 247 CMR 20.02(1) a Manager of Record of a pharmacy shall report to the Board any improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, within seven business days of discovery of serious injury or death related to improper dispensing. Under 247 CMR 20.02(2) a Manager of Record shall report any serious adverse drug event that occurs as a result of a patient's interaction with any drug or pharmaceutical manufactured, produced or compounded at the pharmacy, and that report goes to three recipients: the Board, the Federal Food and Drug Administration MedWatch Program, and the Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction. Its period is also seven business days, but it runs from the knowledge of the serious adverse drug event by any pharmacy employee rather than from the Manager of Record's own discovery. 247 CMR 20.02(3) then closes the obvious shortcut: the duty to report to the Board improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, or a serious adverse drug event, shall be in addition to the Continuous Quality Improvement Program requirements of 247 CMR 15.00.

Before applying any of 247 CMR 20.02, ask which pharmacy the facts are about, because 247 CMR 20.02(5) provides that the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies. The carve-out is not a gap in the scheme: 247 CMR 20.07(1) requires a non-resident pharmacy, non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy and non-resident complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy to comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, and 247 CMR 20.07(3) states the duty that replaces 20.02(1) for them. A non-resident pharmacy shall report to the Board any improper dispensing, into Massachusetts, of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing. The length is the same and the recipient is the same, but the trigger is not. The resident pharmacy's clock runs from discovery of the serious injury or death, and the non-resident pharmacy's runs from discovery of the improper dispensing, so the same facts can produce two different start dates depending on where the pharmacy sits.

A reportable event leaves a longer paper trail than the report itself. 247 CMR 20.02(4) requires a pharmacy to retain all records relating to the improper dispensing of a prescription drug that results in serious injury or death, and all records relating to serious adverse drug events, for a minimum period of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, and it adds that the records shall be readily retrievable. Two details in that sentence do the work. The period runs from the filing of the report and not from the dispensing, the injury or the discovery, so delay in filing lengthens the retention rather than shortening it. And readily retrievable is a standard about the manner of keeping and not merely about duration: material that exists somewhere in an unindexed archive has been retained but is not readily retrievable. The five-year period attaches to all records relating to the event, not only to the copy of the report that was filed.

The third track has nothing to do with the CQI Program. Under 105 CMR 700.008, a Department of Public Health regulation, a registrant shall report the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery of such theft, loss or suspected tampering, by completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for such purpose. Three features separate it from everything else in this section. Suspicion of tampering is itself a trigger, so nothing has to be confirmed missing before the duty attaches. The 24 hours run from discovery rather than from the theft, the loss, or the delivery that later turns out to have been interfered with. And the recipient is the Drug Control Program on its own form, so a report made to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy instead does not answer this regulation. Registrant carries its defined sense here: 105 CMR 700.001 makes it a person registered by the Department under M.G.L. c. 94C, and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) read with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) leaves a retail drug business registered with the Board instead, so the 24-hour route reaches an operator such as a hospital directly.

That the Drug Control Program report does not go to the Board is not the same proposition as a theft or loss never going to the Board, and the difference decides questions. 247 CMR 20.03(7) requires a Drug Store pharmacy, sterile compounding pharmacy, complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy or nuclear pharmacy located in Massachusetts to report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances by submitting to the Board a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 within seven days of such theft or significant loss, and to comply where applicable with the reporting requirements of the DEA, the Department and the state and local police. So a discovered loss of controlled substances at a Massachusetts pharmacy can owe a Board report on a seven-day clock, a Department report on a 24-hour clock where the operator is a Department registrant, and the federal route, which is taught in the section on controlled substance security and disposal. What the 105 CMR 700.008 route rules out is only the substitution of a Board report for the Drug Control Program's form.

Two retention periods run through this material and they are not the same period, so keep them apart by their start points. 247 CMR 15.04(2) gives the ordinary QRE record a minimum of two years from the date of the QRE report, and it reaches every QRE whether or not the event ever becomes reportable to anyone. 247 CMR 20.02(4) gives records relating to a reportable improper dispensing or a serious adverse drug event a minimum of five years from the date the report is filed with the Board, together with a readily retrievable standard the CQI provision does not state. A single serious event therefore sits inside both: the QRE record it generated runs two years from the QRE report, and the wider file of records relating to the event runs five years from the filing. One boundary is worth fixing as well, because it is a place where a plausible proposition would have to come from outside these rules. Nothing in 247 CMR 15.00 makes a QRE record confidential, privileged or shielded from discovery, so this section teaches no such protection, and the internal character of the record is not itself a legal shield. The federal theft-or-loss reporting route is separate law with its own recipient, form and trigger, and it belongs to its own section rather than to this one.
